nameStory: The white-footed mouse gets its name from its distinctive white feet that look like tiny socks against its brown fur. This charming feature makes it easy to distinguish from other small rodents, as if nature gave it permanent white booties to wear through the forest.
description: The white-footed mouse is a small, brownish rodent about the size of your thumb with a body length of 3-4 inches plus a long tail. Its soft fur is rusty-brown to grayish-brown on top with a bright white belly, and those trademark white feet that give it its name. The large, dark eyes and prominent ears give it an alert, almost deer-like appearance. These nimble climbers are common throughout New England's woodlands.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Distinctly white feet and belly contrast sharply with warm brown or grayish-brown back fur that feels soft and dense to the touch

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Small mouse with large, dark eyes and prominent ears; body about 3-4 inches long with a tail nearly as long as the body

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed front prints and five-toed hind prints in soft soil or snow, often showing the distinctive white foot pads

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Excellent climbers that scamper up tree trunks and along branches with surprising agility; active at night with quick, darting movements

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small, rice-grain sized dark droppings near nests; gnaw marks on nuts and seeds; spherical nests of shredded bark and leaves in tree cavities or brush piles

habitat: White-footed mice prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with plenty of fallen logs, brush piles, and tree cavities for nesting. They're especially common in areas with oak, maple, and beech trees that provide abundant nuts and seeds. You'll also find them along wooded edges, stone walls, and old barns or cabins near forested areas.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, with breeding season beginning and young mice dispersing to find new territories. Fresh gnaw marks on early spring nuts and buds become visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with multiple litters being raised. Abundant food sources mean they're less likely to enter buildings, staying mostly in forest habitats.
seasonality.fall: Busy collecting and caching nuts, seeds, and berries for winter storage. You'll see increased gnaw marks on acorns and other mast crops during this hoarding season.
seasonality.winter: Remain active but stay closer to nest sites in tree cavities or protected areas. More likely to enter cabins, sheds, or homes seeking warmth and food.

funFact: White-footed mice are nature's hoarders, sometimes storing over a gallon of nuts and seeds in a single cache, and they can remember the locations of dozens of different food storage sites throughout their territory.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Eastern deermouse, which has a more sharply defined color line between its brown back and white belly, while white-footed mice have a more gradual color transition. Remember: deermouse has a "deer-like" sharp color division.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "woodmouse" in some regions like Texas, this name actually belongs to a completely different European species. The white-footed mouse is a true North American native and part of the diverse deermouse group.
compareHints: White-footed mice have more gradual color transitions and slightly smaller ears compared to their close relative, the Eastern deermouse. The deermouse typically shows a sharper dividing line between its brown back and white underside, creating a more bicolored appearance. Both species have white feet, but deermice often have more contrasting tail coloration with distinct dark tops and white bottoms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative, the White-footed Mouse, the Eastern Deermouse has proportionally larger ears, a more distinct brown-to-white color boundary on its sides, and slightly longer hind feet.
